states.name: Castle
timeline: The castle on its rock, held by a government garrison
The Jacobites hold the town; the castle holds out for the government
The castle remains a government fortress and prison

states.name: Castlehill & Lawnmarket
timeline: Hume is born on 26 April, by tradition in the Lawnmarket
His father dies; the family lives mostly at Ninewells, in Berwickshire
September: the Jacobite army of Charles Edward Stuart takes the town
November: the Jacobite army marches south into England
Hume and his sister take a flat in Riddle's Court, off the Lawnmarket
Hume moves down the hill to the Canongate
Hume buys a flat in James's Court, on the north side of the Lawnmarket
Hume leaves for the British embassy in Paris
Home from London, Hume lives in James's Court again
Hume moves to his new house in the New Town

states.name: High Street & Parliament Close
timeline: The High Street, St Giles' and Parliament Close, the heart of the old town
Charles Edward Stuart is proclaimed regent for his father at the Mercat Cross
November: the Jacobite army marches south into England
Hume becomes Keeper of the Advocates' Library, under Parliament House
The curators strike three of his French books from the library
Hume gives up the library
The Royal Exchange, now the City Chambers, is finished

states.name: Canongate
timeline: The Canongate, a separate burgh below the Netherbow Port
September: the Jacobite army of Charles Edward Stuart takes the town
November: the Jacobite army marches south into England
Hume rents Jack's Land in the Canongate, where he writes much of his History
Hume moves back up to the Lawnmarket
The Netherbow Port, the gate between the two burghs, is pulled down

states.name: Holyrood
timeline: The palace and abbey of Holyroodhouse and the King's Park
Charles Edward Stuart holds court at Holyroodhouse
November: the Jacobite army marches south into England

states.name: Cowgate & Grassmarket
timeline: The Cowgate and the Grassmarket, the low streets south of the ridge
The Porteous Riot: a crowd hangs Captain John Porteous in the Grassmarket
Parliament fines the city for the riot
September: the Jacobite army of Charles Edward Stuart takes the town
November: the Jacobite army marches south into England

states.name: College & South Side
timeline: The Town's College and the South Side
Hume, aged ten to twelve (sources differ), enters the College with his brother
Hume leaves the College without a degree; he is meant to study law
After a year-long contest the town council passes Hume over for the chair of moral philosophy
George Square is laid out on the southern fields

states.name: Meadows & Heriot's
timeline: The Burgh Loch and the fields south of the town
The drained loch is now the Meadows, a walk lined with trees

states.name: West Kirk & West Port fields
timeline: Fields around the West Kirk of St Cuthbert's and the West Port

states.name: Nor' Loch
timeline: The Nor' Loch, the town's foul northern moat
The town begins to drain the Nor' Loch
The foundation stone of the North Bridge is laid across the valley
Part of the unfinished North Bridge collapses; five people die
The North Bridge opens, linking the old town to the new

states.name: Fields of the New Town
timeline: Farmland north of the Nor' Loch
James Craig's plan for a New Town is adopted and building begins
Hume moves into his new house on the corner of St Andrew Square
Hume dies at home on 25 August

states.name: Calton Hill
timeline: Calton Hill, its burial ground and the village of Calton
Hume is buried in the Old Calton burial ground

events.title: Hume is born
events.text: David Home, later Hume, is born in Edinburgh on 26 April, by tradition in the Lawnmarket, the younger son of a Berwickshire laird.

events.title: Father dies
events.text: Joseph Home dies; his widow Katherine Falconer raises the three children, mostly at Ninewells.

events.title: The College
events.text: Aged ten to twelve (sources differ), David follows his brother John to the Town's College.

events.title: Law books
events.text: Meant to be a lawyer, Hume secretly reads Cicero and Virgil instead.

events.title: New scene of thought
events.text: At eighteen, reading at home and in town, Hume glimpses 'a new Scene of Thought'; months of work end in a breakdown.

events.title: Porteous Riot
events.text: A crowd breaks into the Tolbooth and hangs Captain Porteous in the Grassmarket.

events.title: Essays succeed
events.text: Essays, Moral and Political, printed in Edinburgh, sell well.

events.title: No chair for Hume
events.text: After a year-long contest, the town council passes Hume over for the chair of moral philosophy amid charges of irreligion.

events.title: A letter in defence
events.text: A Letter from a Gentleman, printed in Edinburgh, answers the charges against the Treatise.

events.title: Jacobites take the town
events.text: On 17 September the Jacobite army enters Edinburgh; the castle holds out.

events.title: Court at Holyrood
events.text: Charles Edward Stuart holds court at Holyroodhouse until the army marches south.

events.title: The castle holds
events.text: The government garrison keeps the castle throughout the occupation.

events.title: The Provost's defence
events.text: Hume writes a defence of Provost Archibald Stewart, tried for surrendering the town.

events.title: Riddle's Court
events.text: Hume settles in Edinburgh with his sister Katherine, in Riddle's Court.

events.title: Keeper of the library
events.text: Hume becomes Keeper of the Advocates' Library, which gives him 'the command of a large library'.

events.title: Political Discourses
events.text: Hume's Political Discourses, on trade, money and population, are a success.

events.title: Jack's Land
events.text: Hume moves to Jack's Land in the Canongate.

events.title: Royal Exchange
events.text: Building begins on the Royal Exchange, today's City Chambers.

events.title: History of England
events.text: The first volume of Hume's History, on the early Stuarts, is attacked from all sides.

events.title: Banned books
events.text: The library's curators strike three French books Hume had bought as indecent.

events.title: Select Society
events.text: Hume joins the Select Society, a debating club of Edinburgh's lawyers, ministers and scholars.

events.title: The Kirk and Hume
events.text: In the General Assembly, a move to censure Hume's writings fails.

events.title: Leaves the library
events.text: Hume gives up the Advocates' Library.

events.title: Draining the loch
events.text: The town begins to drain the Nor' Loch, opening the way north.

events.title: James's Court
events.text: Hume buys a flat in James's Court, high above the Nor' Loch valley.

events.title: History complete
events.text: The last volumes of the History of England appear; it becomes a best-seller.

events.title: North Bridge
events.text: The foundation stone of the North Bridge is laid while Hume is in Paris.

events.title: Netherbow Port
events.text: The old gate between Edinburgh and the Canongate is pulled down.

events.title: George Square
events.text: Building begins on George Square, south of the College.

events.title: A New Town
events.text: James Craig's plan for a New Town north of the Nor' Loch is adopted.

events.title: Home again
events.text: Hume returns to Edinburgh for good, 'very opulent', he writes.

events.title: Bridge collapse
events.text: Part of the North Bridge falls in August; five people are killed.

events.title: St David Street
events.text: Hume moves into his new house; a later tradition says someone chalked 'St David Street' on its wall.

events.title: Bridge opens
events.text: The North Bridge opens, linking the old town and the new.

events.title: My Own Life
events.text: In April Hume, gravely ill, writes a short autobiography, My Own Life.

events.title: Boswell's visit
events.text: On 7 July James Boswell finds Hume calm about dying and is deeply shaken.

events.title: Death
events.text: Hume dies at home on 25 August, aged sixty-five.

events.title: Burial
events.text: Hume is buried in the Old Calton burial ground; Robert Adam's round tomb follows in 1777–78.

eras: The historian of the Old Town
chartNote: Share of the mapped area of 18th-century Edinburgh, by quarter. Quarters follow William Edgar's plan of the city (1742, revised 1765) and James Craig's New Town plan (1767), placed on today's streets; their boundaries are approximate. A simplification: a colour stands for a whole quarter, though Hume's homes were single flats and his house positions are estimated.
